title: Oedipus and the Enigma
text:
Quadruped in the dawn, tall in the day,
+        and with three feet wandering through the vain
+        realm of evening: so the eternal sphinx
+        saw her inconstant brother,
+
+
+        man; and with evening came a man
+        who deciphered, terrified, in the mirror
+        of the monstrous image, the reflection
+        of his decline and of his fate.
+
+
+        We are Oedipus, and in an eternal way
+        we are the long and triple beast, all
+        that we shall be and all that we have been.
+
+
+        To see the huge form of our being
+        would annihilate us; mercifully,
+        God grants us succession and oblivion.
editorial_note: The riddle becomes a metaphysical self-portrait: humanity is spared total vision of itself by temporal succession and forgetfulness.

title: The Borgeses
text:
Nothing, or very little, do I know of my Portuguese
+        forebears, the Borgeses: a vague people
+        who continue in my flesh, obscurely,
+        their habits, rigors, and fears.
+
+
+        Faint as if they had never been,
+        and alien to the proceedings of art,
+        they form, indecipherably, part
+        of time, of earth, and of oblivion.
+
+
+        Better so. Their labor done,
+        they are Portugal, they are the famous people
+        who forced the walls of the Orient
+
+
+        and gave themselves to the sea and the other sea of sand.
+        They are the king who in the mystic desert
+        was lost, and the one who swears he has not died.
editorial_note: Genealogy becomes indistinct inheritance in flesh and history; the closing alludes to Sebastianic myth without overexplaining Borges’s compressed national memory.

title: Elegy for the Fatherland
text:
Of iron, not of gold, was the dawn.
+        A port and a desert forged it,
+        a handful of gentlemen and the open
+        elemental realm of yesterday and now.
+
+
+        Then came the war against the Goth.
+        Always courage and always victory.
+        Brazil and the tyrant. That unbridled
+        history. Everything staked on everything.
+
+
+        Red numerals of anniversaries,
+        pomps of marble, arduous monuments,
+        pomps of the word, parliaments,
+
+
+        centennials and sesquicentennials,
+        are scarcely the ash, the harangue,
+        of the vestiges of that ancient flame.
editorial_note: The patriotic rhetoric is treated skeptically: commemorative marble and speeches are only ash and soflama beside the older historical flame.

title: Afternoon That Undermined Our Farewell…
text:
Afternoon that undermined our farewell.
+
+Steely and delightful afternoon, monstrous as a dark angel.
+
+Afternoon when our lips lived in the naked intimacy of kisses.
+
+Inevitable time overflowed
+
+over the useless embrace.
+
+Together we lavished passion, not for ourselves but for the solitude already near.
+
+The light rejected us; night had arrived urgently.
+
+We went to the gate in that gravity of shadow already eased by the evening star.
+
+Like one returning from a lost meadow, I returned from your embrace.
+
+Like one returning from a country of swords, I returned from your tears.
+
+Afternoon that endures, vivid as a dream,
+
+among the other afternoons.
+
+Afterward I kept reaching and passing beyond
+
+nights and sea-days.
editorial_note: The young Borges’s long prose-verse sentence keeps its exalted abstraction; singladuras becomes sea-days to preserve voyaging time after the farewell.

title: Brunanburh, 937 A.D.
text:
No one beside you.
+
+Last night I killed a man in battle.
+
+He was brave and tall, of the clear lineage of Anlaf.
+
+The sword entered his breast, a little to the left.
+
+He rolled to the earth and was a thing,
+
+a thing for the raven.
+
+In vain you will wait for him, woman I have not seen.
+
+The ships that fled
+
+over the yellow water will not bring him.
+
+At the hour of dawn,
+
+your hand, from sleep, will seek him.
+
+Your bed is cold.
+
+Last night I killed a man at Brunanburh.
+
+
+
+
+Author’s note: Brunanburgh. These are the words of a Saxon who fought in the victory the kings of Wessex won over a coalition of Scots, Danes, and Britons, commanded by Anlaf (Olaf) of Ireland. In the poem there are echoes of the contemporary ode that Tennyson so admirably translated.
editorial_note: The voice is kept stark and Anglo-Saxon in its repetitions; cosa del cuervo becomes thing for the raven, preserving the corpse’s conversion into battle spoil.

title: Where Is the Memory of the Days…
text:
Where is the memory of the days
+
+that were yours on earth, and wove
+
+happiness and pain and were the universe to you?
+
+
+The numerable river of the years
+
+has lost them; you are a word in an index.
+
+
+The gods gave others endless glory,
+
+inscriptions and exergues and monuments and punctual historians;
+
+of you we know only, obscure friend,
+
+that you heard the nightingale one afternoon.
+
+
+Among the asphodels of shadow, your vain shade
+
+will think the gods have been miserly.
+
+
+But days are a net of trivial miseries,
+
+and what better fortune could there be than to be the ash
+
+of which oblivion is made?
+
+
+Upon others the gods cast
+
+the inexorable light of glory, which looks into the entrails and counts the cracks,
+
+of glory, which ends by tarnishing the rose it venerates;
+
+with you they were more merciful, brother.
+
+
+In the ecstasy of an evening that will not become night,
+
+you hear the voice of Theocritus’s nightingale.
editorial_note: The poem’s consolation is paradoxical: anonymity is a mercy beside glory’s destructive scrutiny, leaving only the nightingale as sufficient destiny.

title: Heraclitus
text:
Heraclitus walks through the evening
+
+of Ephesus. Evening has left him,
+
+without his will deciding it,
+
+on the bank of a silent river
+
+whose destiny and whose name he does not know.
+
+There is a stone Janus and some poplars.
+
+He looks at himself in the fugitive mirror
+
+and discovers and fashions the sentence
+
+that the generations of men
+
+will not let fall. His voice declares:
+
+No one steps twice into the waters
+
+of the same river. He stops. He feels,
+
+with the amazement of a sacred horror,
+
+that he too is a river and a flight.
+
+He wants to recover that morning
+
+and his night and the eve before. He cannot.
+
+He repeats the sentence. He sees it printed
+
+in future and clear characters
+
+on one of Burnet’s pages.
+
+Heraclitus does not know Greek. Janus,
+
+god of gates, is a Latin god.
+
+Heraclitus has no yesterday or now.
+
+He is a mere artifice dreamed
+
+by a gray man on the banks of the Red Cedar,
+
+a man who interweaves hendecasyllables
+
+so as not to think so much of Buenos Aires
+
+and of beloved faces. One is missing.
editorial_note: The poem’s anachronisms are kept explicit: the philosopher is a literary artifice invented by Borges, whose river is also exile and bereavement.

text:

editorial_note: This titled witness uses the same reviewed diction as the first-line version, while preserving the indented anthology layout.
